title: What social teaching is
hook: a pope writes a letter about wages, strikes and the poor, and a new strand of teaching begins

segments.voice: Yesterday the great orders closed: Benedict, Francis, Dominic, Ignatius, Carmel. Your line was many rooms, one house. Did one room start to feel like yours? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

No incense today. No cloister. Today starts with a paycheck that runs out before the month does, a factory floor, a landlord at the door. A pope, Leo the Thirteenth, wrote a long letter about exactly those things: workers and owners, wages and strikes, property and the poor. It opens with two Latin words, rerum novarum, of new things, and those words became its name. The new things were the changes in work and cities that Leo saw around him. A new block of the path begins with that letter, and with a phrase for the teaching that grew from it. Today, Catholic social teaching.
screen: `A PAYCHECK, A FACTORY, A LANDLORD.` → `A POPE WRITES ABOUT WAGES.` → `RERUM NOVARUM: OF NEW THINGS.`

segments.voice: First, what the phrase names. Catholic social teaching isn't one book. It's a body of teaching built up from letters by popes, from councils and from bishops, and gathered in the Catechism, about how a society should be ordered so that people can flourish in it. Wages, housing, war, migration, the earth itself. Second, where it comes from. The Church says it isn't a new invention bolted onto the faith. It grows from the conviction that every person is made in God's image, and from Jesus' own words about feeding the hungry and welcoming the stranger. Leo carried that old conviction onto the new factory floor. Third, the line that holds the spirit of it. The first letter of John says, in the Douay-Rheims: "My little children, let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth." Social teaching is that sentence, scaled up. Helping the one neighbor at your door is charity, and the Church never stops asking for it. Asking why so many neighbors keep coming to the same door, and what could change that, is where social teaching begins. That's what today's line means by love, organized. Fourth, what it isn't. John Paul the Second wrote that the Church doesn't offer technical solutions or a political program. It offers principles, and leaves the hard work of applying them to people in each place, who may disagree about how. Catholics can land on different sides of a political argument and still be asked to measure their choices by the same principles. Over the coming days this block takes them one at a time: dignity, community, rights and duties, the poor, work, solidarity, creation.
screen: `A BODY OF TEACHING, NOT ONE BOOK.` · `GROWN FROM THE IMAGE OF GOD.` · then, large: `NOT IN WORD, BUT IN DEED.` · then: `PRINCIPLES, NOT A PARTY PLATFORM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you can find the text of Rerum Novarum, read one paragraph of it slowly, any paragraph, before the sit. If not, take the line from John instead: not in word, but in deed. Then settle, and breathe. Let one question come up and stay: where in my week does care stay at the level of words? A cause that gets talked about and never touched. A problem met one person at a time that might have a root somewhere. Don't solve it. Just see it clearly. If you pray, you can bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Catholic social teaching. The Church's body of teaching on justice in society, from Leo's letter on: love put to work in the way a society is built. Today's word.
Your line: love, organized. Today, pick one problem you usually meet one person at a time, and ask what would make it smaller for the people who come after. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Catholics meet social teaching in papal letters called encyclicals, in the Catechism, in homilies, and in parish and diocesan work for the poor, workers and migrants; some parishes run study groups on it.

fork.setup: you're a pope, and the questions on your desk are wages, strikes, property and the poor. what do you do?
options: leave it alone: the Church sticks to prayer.
write a letter on workers and owners, grounded in the faith.
draw up a detailed economic plan every country must adopt.
fork.reveal: Leo XIII wrote Rerum Novarum. it gave principles, not a blueprint, and later popes said plainly that the Church offers no technical solutions.

original.note: Latin: of new things. the opening words of Leo XIII's letter, and so its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Church's opinions about politics.
what it means: a body of teaching on how a society should be ordered so every person can flourish, grown from the gospel.
what a scholar hears: John Paul II's insistence that it isn't an ideology or a third way between systems, but belongs to moral theology.

notes: No date given in the voice for Rerum Novarum; the index hook's 'since 1891' is left out under the claims rule. The title of the block is unchanged.
Claim: 'It opens with two Latin words, rerum novarum ... and those words became its name.' Confirm the Latin incipit (Rerum novarum semel excitata cupidine).

Paraphrase of Sollicitudo Rei Socialis 41: the Church does not offer technical solutions; its social doctrine is not an ideology or a 'third way' and belongs to moral theology. Confirm the trapdoor wording.
Distinction between charity and social teaching ('why so many keep coming to the same door') is an interpretive framing, not a quotation; confirm it fits CCC 2419–2449.
Practice invites reading Rerum Novarum; English translations on the Vatican site may be under copyright, so nothing from it is quoted.
